CausalChain: Oxidative stress -> Upregulation of HBXIP -> Activation/upregulation of METTL3 -> Enhanced m6A modification on metabolic transcripts and HIF-1α mRNA // Oxidative stress -> Activation of METTL3/METTL14 -> Selective m6A tagging of hypoxia-responsive lncRNAs (e.g., lncRNA-X) -> Increased binding of IGF2BP2 -> Stabilization of HIF-1α mRNA -> Elevated HIF-1α protein -> Angiogenesis and further oxidative stress
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that in HCC, oxidative stress drives tumor progression through two interconnected regulatory axes. One axis involves the well-established HBXIP-mediated upregulation of METTL3, which enhances m6A modifications on key metabolic transcripts and directly on HIF-1α mRNA, thereby contributing to metabolic reprogramming and tumor growth. A novel, complementary axis is proposed in which oxidative stress directly activates METTL3/METTL14 to selectively modify a specific subset of hypoxia-responsive lncRNAs, such as lncRNA-X. This epitranscriptomic modification increases the binding affinity of these lncRNAs for IGF2BP2, leading to the stabilization of HIF-1α mRNA. The resultant accumulation of HIF-1α protein not only drives angiogenesis but also reinforces oxidative stress, forming a self-amplifying loop. This refined model, which integrates classical HBXIP-METTL3 mechanisms with innovative lncRNA-dependent stabilization pathways, will be rigorously tested using contemporary technologies including m6A-seq for mapping methylation, CLIP-seq for profiling lncRNA-RBP interactions, and CRISPR-based epitranscriptomic interventions for targeted modulation in vitro and in vivo.
Abstract: In hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), multifaceted regulatory networks drive tumor progression through both metabolic reprogramming and epitranscriptomic modifications. We propose a revised dual-pathway hypothesis wherein oxidative stress initiates two convergent regulatory cascades. First, oxidative stress enhances HBXIP expression which, in turn, upregulates METTL3, augmenting m6A methylation on critical metabolic transcripts and HIF-1α mRNA. Second, a distinct mechanism is activated whereby oxidative stress, through increased activity of METTL3/METTL14, selectively modifies a subset of hypoxia-responsive long noncoding RNAs (e.g., candidate lncRNA-X). The m6A tagging of these lncRNAs augments their binding affinity for the RNA-binding protein IGF2BP2, leading to the stabilization of HIF-1α mRNA. Elevated HIF-1α protein levels then drive angiogenesis and further exacerbate oxidative stress, establishing a self-amplifying loop. This model will be interrogated using advanced techniques such as m6A-seq, CLIP-seq, and CRISPR-based epitranscriptomic editing, which together enable precise dissection of these interconnected pathways and their contributions to HCC progression.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis posited that oxidative stress upregulates METTL3/METTL14 leading to enhanced m6A modifications on hypoxia-responsive lncRNAs which interact with IGF2BP2 to stabilize HIF-1α mRNA. Our revised hypothesis maintains this core causal chain but integrates recent observations by incorporating the HBXIP-mediated pathway that upregulates METTL3 and influences m6A modifications on metabolic transcripts. We now propose a dual-axis mechanism that acknowledges established evidence for HBXIP involvement and the role of m6A on serine synthesis pathway enzymes (via IGF2BP3) while also delineating a novel, selective pathway where oxidative stress leads to targeted m6A modification of lncRNA-X, boosting IGF2BP2 binding and HIF-1α mRNA stabilization. Additionally, we enhance practical implementability by specifying the use of state-of-the-art m6A-seq, CLIP-seq, and CRISPR-based epitranscriptomic editing, thereby refining and extending the causal reasoning of the original model.
